Chapter seven. The number that matters.

Here it is. Thirty-seven thousand euros.

That's the difference between investor A and investor B. Same money, same index, same start date, same crash.

The only difference was one decision, made in a moment of fear. That's the price of panic.

No ETF, no equal weighting, no clever strategy came anywhere close to that number in this replay. Your behaviour mattered more than your fund.

Let's recap what the euro data showed us.

Buying at the dot-com top: forty-five percent down, and thirteen years to get back to even.

The dollar: it can add a second punch of up to forty percent, or soften the blow.

Swapping one stock index for another: helps in a tech-only correction, barely matters in a full crash.

A sixty forty with euro bonds: back to even eight years sooner, for a smaller final result.

The monthly saver: money multiplied by more than four. And panic selling: a thirty-seven thousand euro mistake.

And this isn't just my replay. Morningstar's yearly Mind the Gap study keeps finding the same thing: investors earn less than the funds they own, because they buy after the rises and sell after the falls.

So, is AI a bubble? Honestly, I don't know. And neither does anyone on YouTube who tells you they do.

And even if it is a bubble, that doesn't mean AI is fake. The internet wasn't fake either. Amazon survived the dot-com crash and became one of the biggest companies on Earth.

But between 1999 and 2001, Amazon's share price still fell by more than ninety percent. Being right about the technology is not the same as being right about the price.

The E C B thinks a correction is likely. But bubbles can also run much longer than anyone expects. In 1996, Alan Greenspan warned about irrational exuberance. The Nasdaq then almost quadrupled before it crashed.

What I do know is this: we have twenty-seven years of real euro data, two full bubbles, and the same lesson every single time.

The crash itself never decided who ended up rich. What people did during the crash did.

So instead of predicting, here's what I'd check in my own portfolio. This is not financial advice, just a checklist.

One. Look at your ETF's top ten and its country weights. Know what you actually own.

Two. Set your mix of stocks and bonds by when you need the money, not by the headlines.

Three. If you diversify away from the giants, do it for the long run, knowing it can lag for a decade.

Four. Automate your monthly plan, so a scary headline can't stop it.

And five. Write down today what you will do if your portfolio drops forty percent. Decide now, while you're calm.

Question three. And be honest. If your portfolio dropped forty-five percent next year, what would you do?

A, sell. B, stop buying. Or C, keep going. Tell me in the comments.

If you want to see how a crash right before retirement changes everything, watch my video where I simulated ten thousand European retirements. It's on my channel.

And if you want more real euro data instead of hype, subscribe. Every video on this channel is built on numbers you can check.

Thanks for watching. See you in the next one.
